identification.summary: SpaceBears (also written Space Bears) is a double-extortion ransomware and data-leak operation that appeared in 2024 and is aligned with the Phobos ransomware-as-a-service ecosystem [S1][S2]. It is believed to operate from Moscow, though sources caution this is hard to confirm [S2]. Trackers describe it as targeting small and medium organizations in the US and Europe [S4].
identification.firstObserved: April 2024: S-RM first identified a Faust operator, a Phobos affiliate, using a new leak site called 'Space Bears' [S1][S2].
identification.notes: No Microsoft name or MITRE group ID exists for this actor in the sources gathered. Some sources describe it as a data broker rather than a ransomware operator, and assessments of its sophistication differ [S2]. Do not merge facts with Phobos or Faust/8Base clusters; the sources state alignment/affiliate use of the leak site, not that they are the same actor [S1].

attribution.confidence: Vendors and trackers (SOCRadar, ransomware.live) list the source country as Russia; the Moscow location is described as believed but hard to confirm [S2][S4][S5]. No government attribution found.
attribution.basis: Leak-site observation by S-RM linking the site to a Phobos affiliate [S1]; tracker country labels [S4][S5].

objectives: Financial gain through double extortion: encrypting data and threatening to publish stolen files if no ransom is paid [S2][S5].

targeting.notes: ransomware.live snapshot lists 123 victims, with the US at 38 and business services (23), healthcare (19) and technology (18) leading; SOCRadar snapshots show roughly 56 to 62 victims, so counts conflict and are automatically generated [S4][S5]. Earlier press counts were just over 30 (The Record) and over 40 (SecurityWeek), as relayed by Infosecurity Magazine coverage [S2].

capabilities.summary: Operates a corporate-styled data leak site (stock imagery, business language) used to host and publish stolen data, with S-RM noting Phobos teams use this site and that it remains unclear whether it is their exclusive leak site [S1][S2]. Reported initial access includes social engineering, phishing and exploitation of known software vulnerabilities, per SOCRadar [S5]. SOCRadar characterizes it as relying on basic extortion rather than sophisticated malware, while a Basque CERT report calls it sophisticated; these assessments conflict [S2].

campaigns.name: Leak site first observed
campaigns.summary: S-RM identified a Faust (Phobos affiliate) operator using a new leak site named 'Space Bears'.

campaigns.name: Claim against Atos
campaigns.summary: Space Bears listed Atos on its site and pledged to publish data in early January 2025 (reports differ between 7 and 8 January). Atos said initial analysis showed no compromise of its systems and no ransom demand; it later called the claims unfounded while acknowledging third-party infrastructure containing its name was compromised.

diamond.adversary: Ransomware/extortion group believed to be Moscow-based, aligned with Phobos RaaS [S1][S2].
diamond.capability: Double extortion, data theft and leak-site publication; phishing and known-vulnerability exploitation reported by secondary sources [S2][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Corporate-themed data leak site on which stolen data is hosted [S1][S2]. Other infrastructure not documented in gathered sources.
diamond.victim: Small and medium organizations, mainly US and Europe, in business services, healthcare, technology, manufacturing and construction [S4].
diamond.socioPolitical: Financially motivated criminal activity; no state sponsorship stated in sources [S5].
diamond.technology: Unpatched internet-facing systems and phishing-susceptible users, per SOCRadar [S5].

gaps: Relationship to Phobos, Faust and 8Base operators is stated only as alignment or affiliate use of the leak site; the exact organizational link is unverified [S1].
Moscow location is believed but not confirmed [S2].
Victim counts conflict across trackers (about 30 to 123); no authoritative tally [S2][S4][S5].
Atos claim was not backed by public evidence of compromise; Atos disputes it [S2].

Could not open primary vendor pages (SOCRadar dark web profile, Tripwire, The Record, Halcyon, Cyberzaintza PDF); details are drawn from search-result summaries and the S-RM, Infosecurity and tracker pages listed. The TTP statements (phishing, vulnerability exploitation) need verification against primary write-ups.
No malware family, encryptor, C2 or IOC data collected; no government advisory or MITRE profile found.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Healthcare, technology and business-service networks of small and mid-sized organizations, including DIB suppliers of similar size, are the exposed terrain; unpatched internet-facing systems and phishing exposure are the key access points [S4][S5]. STEP 2: Low-sophistication extortion lowers the adversary's cost and favors volume over precision; the corporate leak site is the pressure channel [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Observed pattern is initial access by phishing or exposed services, data theft, encryption, then leak-site listing and publication deadline [S2][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued opportunistic extortion of small and medium US and European organizations. MDCOA is a supplier or managed-service provider compromise whose data is published to embarrass or pressure a larger customer, as the Atos claim attempted via third-party infrastructure [S2]. Candidate indicators: new victim postings on the leak site, and mass file encryption or exfiltration from small supplier networks [S1][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: monitor leak-site postings naming DIB suppliers, vendors and partners, and verify claims before reacting since claims can be unsupported [S2]. (2) Authorities: criminal ransomware response runs through law enforcement and DC3/DIB reporting channels rather than offensive cyber authorities; confirm with legal. (3) Mission assurance: identify mission-relevant suppliers using small-organization networks and confirm patching and backup posture. (4) Coordination: share indicators with industry and allied CERTs; third-party data exposure can mention a larger organization's name without compromising its own systems [S2].

Atos Group Denies Space Bears' Ransomware Attack Claims (relaying Halcyon, SOCRadar, S-RM, The Record, SecurityWeek)

provenance.importedSummary: SpaceBears is a ransomware group believed to be based in Moscow, Russia, that has taken credit for several high-profile cyberattacks while primarily operating as a Data Broker. They currently list eight organizations on their Data Leak Site, focusing on medium to small-sized targets. Their methods suggest a reliance on basic extortion strategies rather than sophisticated malware tactics, with no advanced techniques or indicators of ransomware detected.
